slides.title: Bugs and debugging
slides.say: A bug is a place where a program does something other than what its author meant it to do, and debugging is the work of finding and removing such places. Chapter 5 opens with the observation that once a learner can write basic programs, the bugs become less simple, and it offers tools and techniques for finding the root cause of a bug quickly and with little effort (Sweigart, 2025). This branch collects the ideas that sit underneath those tools: what a bug is, how bugs differ from one another, what debugging asks of the programmer, and how to choose the right tool for a given question. Every programmer writes bugs, however experienced. The chapter quotes the old joke that writing code accounts for 90 percent of programming while debugging accounts for the other 90 percent, and it reminds the reader that a computer does only what it is told and will not read the programmer's mind (Sweigart, 2025). A learner who treats debugging as an ordinary, learnable activity, and not as a sign of failure, finds bugs faster and loses less confidence while doing so. The ideas of this branch apply to every program in the course, from a ten-line exercise to the capstone project. They are placed first in the chapter's concept tree because the four groups that follow, raising exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger, are four answers to one question: how can the programmer find out what the program is really doing, as opposed to what its source code appears to say? The branch has three parts. The first describes the nature of a bug, with the bug itself, the logic error that produces a wrong answer without any complaint from Python, and the process of debugging. The second explains how to choose among the four instruments by the question that is being asked. The third, the working vocabulary, explains objects, the command line and files, which the tools take for granted. The chapter gives the guiding rule in its introduction: in general, the earlier a bug is caught, the easier it is to fix (Sweigart, 2025). This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Nature of a bug
slides.say: The nature of a bug concerns what kind of thing a bug is and how it shows itself. Python distinguishes errors that stop a program before it starts, errors that stop it while it runs, and mistakes that do not stop it at all. The first two are reported by the interpreter, and the third is noticed only by a person who sees that the result is wrong. Knowing which of the three kinds one is facing decides what to do next. A message from Python names a line to look at, whereas a silently wrong answer gives no line at all, and the programmer must observe the program's behaviour to find the cause. The chapter's two practice programs, a factorial that returns 0 and an adding program that prints 5342, are both of the silent kind (Sweigart, 2025). The next three concepts take the three kinds in turn: the bug as a gap between intention and behaviour, the logic error that hides behind a program that runs normally, and debugging as the method by which the gap is located and closed. slides.title: Bug
slides.say: The idea matters because it moves the blame to where the repair can happen. A programmer who believes that the computer is wrong looks in the wrong place, whereas a programmer who accepts that the instructions were not the intended ones starts reading them critically. The chapter adds that even professional programmers create bugs all the time, so a learner should not be discouraged by them (Sweigart, 2025). Bugs are met in every program a learner writes. The chapter's first example is a function that computes the factorial of 5, the product 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 x 5, which should be 120. Its loop starts at 0 instead of 1, so the first multiplication multiplies by zero and every later step keeps the total at zero, and the function returns 0 (Sweigart, 2025). The effect can be reproduced by hand. The expression 1 * 0 * 1 * 2 * 3 * 4 * 5, which is the sequence of multiplications that the faulty loop performs, evaluates to 0, because any number multiplied by zero is zero. Nothing in the program is syntactically wrong and no rule of the language is broken, so Python has no reason to complain; the defect exists only relative to what the author wanted. Not every surprising result is a bug in the program: sometimes the author's expectation is wrong. Before changing code, state precisely what the correct result should be and why. Equally, a program that produces the expected output for one input may still contain a bug that shows itself on another, so a bug is confirmed or ruled out by testing more than one case. slides.title: Logic error
slides.say: Logic errors are the hardest bugs to find because nothing points at them. The chapter's adding program shows this clearly: the author remarks that the program has not crashed, but the sum is obviously wrong (Sweigart, 2025). The program's output looks plausible to the interpreter and implausible only to a person who knows what the answer should be. The chapter contains two logic errors. The factorial function returns 0 because its loop begins at the wrong number, and the adding program prints The sum is 5342 for the inputs 5, 3 and 42, because input returns strings and the plus sign joins strings instead of adding numbers (Sweigart, 2025). The coin toss practice program at the end of the chapter contains further ones. Finding a logic error is a matter of making the program show its inner state. The three tools that follow in the chapter do this in different ways: log messages print values as the program runs, assertions check beliefs about values, and the debugger lets the programmer stop the program and read the values. In the adding program, converting each answer with int changes the output from The sum is 5342 to The sum is 50. A passing run is not proof of correctness. A logic error can hide for as long as the test inputs happen not to touch it, so the cheapest defence is to test with inputs whose answers are known in advance and to compare them with what the program prints. slides.title: Debugging
slides.say: A systematic method saves time compared with changing code at random. The chapter notes that the debugger runs a program much more slowly than normal, but lets the programmer see the actual values in a program while it runs, instead of deducing them from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Seeing replaces guessing, and that is the central idea of debugging. Debugging is done at every stage of development: while writing a function and testing it on one input, after a bug report from a user, and while reading someone else's code. The four instruments of the chapter correspond to four moments of this work: a function can refuse bad input with a raised exception, a program can state its beliefs with assertions, a program can leave a record with log messages, and the programmer can stop it with a debugger. A debugging session follows a loop: reproduce the wrong behaviour, look at the program's state at a suitable point, guess the cause, change one thing and run again. The cheapest way to look at the state is a print of the loop's variables. A loop that multiplies a total by i over range(5 + 1) prints 0 0, 1 0, 2 0, 3 0, 4 0 and 5 0 for i and total, and the first line already reveals that i starts at zero. Change one thing at a time, and run the program again after each change; two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one mattered. Remove the temporary prints when the bug is found, or use logging, which the chapter recommends for the reason that its messages can be switched off in one place (Sweigart, 2025).

slides.title: Instrument selection
slides.say: Instrument selection is the choice of which of the chapter's four tools suits a given question. The chapter closes its summary by listing them together: assertions, exceptions, logging and the debugger are all valuable tools to find and prevent bugs (Sweigart, 2025). They overlap but they are not interchangeable, because each answers a different question about a program. A learner who knows only one tool will use it for everything, filling a program with print calls or stepping through a thousand iterations by hand. Matching the tool to the question saves effort and avoids the characteristic misuse of each, such as an assertion that checks what a user types. The next concept states the rule of choice in a sentence for each tool. The branches that follow in the concept tree then explain each tool in turn, beginning with the raise statement. slides.title: Choosing by question
slides.say: The choice matters because each tool has a cost and a purpose. An exception is part of the program's normal behaviour and the user can meet it. An assertion is a check for the programmer, and the chapter says a user should never see an assertion error in a finished program. A log message costs a call but can be switched off with one line, and the debugger costs time at every step. In practice the four tools appear in the same program. A function validates its arguments and raises an exception when the caller made a mistake. An assertion checks an internal result such as a sorted list. Log messages describe the path a long run takes, and the debugger is brought in for the one place where the values still puzzle the programmer. The rule of thumb, which this course states in four sentences, is as follows. Raise an exception when the caller can do something about the error. Assert a condition that must be true if the program is correct. Log when a run must leave a record that can be read after it ends. Step through with the debugger when the question is about the state at one particular line. Each sentence has a concept of its own later in this chapter. The sentences describe tendencies and not laws. A logged message about a user error is often worth keeping next to the exception that reports it, and a debugger session often ends with a new assertion added to keep the bug from returning. Do not use an assertion for a user error, because assertions can be removed from a running program, which a later concept explains.

slides.title: Working vocabulary
slides.say: The working vocabulary gathers three everyday ideas that the chapter's tools take for granted: objects with their attributes and methods, the command line, and files with the directories that hold them. None of them is a tool for finding bugs. Each is needed to read the sentences in which the tools are described, such as the exception stores its arguments in an attribute, run the program with python -m pdb, or the log messages are written to a file. A reader who does not know these words meets them everywhere in the rest of the chapter and in the Python documentation, which uses them without comment. The glossary of the documentation defines them in a line or two, and the course builds on those definitions. Knowing them also removes a source of confusion in debugging itself: a program started from a button of an editor and the same program started from the command line can differ in options and in environment, and a log file that was written in one directory is not found in another. The three concepts take the ideas in turn. The first explains objects, classes, attributes and methods, the vocabulary of every exception, logger and record. The second explains the command line, with its options and arguments, which controls how Python and its debugger are started. The third explains files, their modes, and directories, which the logging branch relies on when it writes a log file. Each has a short executed example. slides.title: Objects, attributes and methods
slides.say: The tools of this chapter are made of objects. An exception is an object that is created by calling a class, and it carries its message in an attribute. A logger, a handler and a log record are objects too, and the list method sort() that the chapter calls on its list of ages is a method of a list object (Sweigart, 2025). Sentences such as the exception stores its arguments in the attribute args, or call the logger's setLevel method, can be read only by a reader who knows what an attribute and a method are. The executed checks show the vocabulary at work. The expression Exception('m') creates an instance, type(Exception('m')).__name__ is 'Exception', and isinstance(Exception('m'), Exception) is True. The attribute args of Exception('custom message') is the tuple ('custom message',). The string 'abc' is an object whose method upper, called as 'abc'.upper(), returns 'ABC', and hasattr(Exception('m'), 'add_note') is True, which says that an exception object has a method with that name. The dotted name reaches into the object. After the dot comes either an attribute, which is a value, or a method, which is called by adding parentheses and arguments. The glossary's statement about the first argument can be checked: 'abc'.upper() and str.upper('abc') both return 'ABC', the second call passing the instance explicitly where the first passes it by the dot. A module is reached in the same way, which is why random.randint and logging.debug are written with a dot. The parentheses decide what the expression means. args is a value, so Exception('m').args() raises a TypeError with the message 'tuple' object is not callable. And 'abc'.upper without parentheses is not an error, but it is not the result either: it is the method itself, whose text starts with <built-in method upper of str object. A call that appears to do nothing is often a method written without its parentheses. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Command line
slides.say: Several tools of this chapter are controlled from the command line. The option -O switches assertions off, python -m pdb main.py runs a program under the debugger, python -m pdb -p followed by a process identifier attaches to a running program, and the setting PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 is placed in the environment of the command. An editor's Run and Debug buttons hide the command line, but the choices it expresses are still there, and a student who knows them can reproduce a run exactly. The command line is met whenever a program is started outside an editor. In the executed check, the command python -c followed by import sys; print(sys.argv) and the two arguments a and b prints ['-c', 'a', 'b'], and a script saved as main.py and started with the same two arguments prints ['main.py', 'a', 'b']. The first item is the name that stands for the program, and the rest are the arguments, in the order typed. The position of a word decides who reads it. Words before the script name or the -c command are options for Python itself. Words after them are arguments for the program, which reads them in sys.argv. Executed check: a script that prints sys.flags.optimize and sys.argv and is started as python main.py -O prints 0 and ['main.py', '-O'], so the -O reached the program and did not switch optimisation on. A misplaced option is silently taken as an argument. python main.py -O does not run the program with assertions off, and in the executed check python -m pdb main.py -O hands -O to the program being debugged, which prints 0 ['main.py', '-O'], and not to Python. The documentation's own description of the interpreter's options is the place to check where an option belongs.

slides.title: File and directory
slides.say: The logging branch writes to files, and several settings of the debugger and of the editors keep their data in files as well. A student has to know where a file is written and what writing it does to an older file with the same name. The tutorial states that mode 'w' erases an existing file with the same name, whereas 'a' adds to the end of it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A log that is written with 'w' every time keeps only the last run, and a log written with 'a' keeps every run. In the chapter the file is the log file: logging.basicConfig(filename='myProgramLog.txt', ...) saves the log messages to that file instead of showing them on the screen (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed check a file is written with the mode 'w' twice, with the texts one and two, and then reads back as two only; after a write in mode 'a' of three, the file holds the two words two and three. The type of the open file is TextIOWrapper, the class of a text file object. A file is used in three steps: open, read or write, close. The tutorial says that in text mode strings are read and written, encoded in a specific encoding, and recommends encoding='utf-8' unless a different one is needed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The glossary explains that to store a string it has to be serialized as a sequence of bytes, and the text encoding is the rule for that. A name without a directory, such as 'workfile', is looked for in the current working directory, which the executed check confirms by finding os.getcwd() to be a directory. The filename alone does not say where a file is. The same name in another directory is another file, so a program that is started from a different directory writes its log somewhere else. Opening an existing file for writing destroys its contents, as the mode 'w' does, and there is no undo. And a file that was not closed may not have its last data written; closing it, as the tutorial's examples do, makes sure that it has.

slides.title: Error signalling
slides.say: Error signalling is the way a program says that something has gone wrong. In Python the saying is done with exceptions: an exception is an object that carries a description of the problem and travels up through the running code until something handles it. Python raises exceptions by itself whenever it tries to execute invalid code, and the programmer can raise them deliberately with the raise statement (Sweigart, 2025). A program that cannot say what went wrong cannot be repaired, either by its author or by its user. Signalling also separates two jobs that belong in different places: the code that notices a problem and the code that decides what to do about it. The chapter states the point plainly: it is often the code that calls a function, and not the function itself, that knows how to handle an exception (Sweigart, 2025). Every Python program meets error signalling, usually first as a traceback printed on the screen after a crash. The chapter extends the earlier treatment of try and except, which handled exceptions that Python raised, with the other half of the story: raising exceptions on purpose and reading what an unhandled one prints (Sweigart, 2025). This branch has two parts. The first, raising, shows how a function refuses a call it cannot serve, which class of exception to choose, how the message travels with the exception and what happens if nobody handles it. The second, tracebacks, explains the record that an exception leaves as it passes through the call stack, and how to read it, including the finer marks and the notes that recent versions of Python add. slides.title: Raising
slides.say: Raising is the act of signalling an exception on purpose. The chapter's section Raising Exceptions explains that raising an exception is a way of saying: stop running this code, and move the program execution to the except statement (Sweigart, 2025). The code that raises does not know who will handle the problem, only that it cannot continue. Raising turns a silent wrong answer into a loud, early failure. A function that is given an argument it cannot work with has only two honest choices, to return something misleading or to refuse, and raising is the refusal. The caller, which knows the larger context, can then recover, ask the user again or stop. The concepts that follow describe the statement itself, the exception classes from which a raiser chooses, the message that is passed along, the use of raising to validate the arguments of a function, and the outcome when no handler exists. slides.title: Raise statement
slides.say: The statement lets a function enforce its own requirements. The chapter's function box_print draws a box from a character, a width and a height, and it raises an exception when the symbol is not one character long or when the width or the height is not greater than 2. Without those checks the function would draw a meaningless shape or fail later in a way that is harder to trace (Sweigart, 2025). A raise statement is typically written inside a function, and the try and except statements that handle the exception are written in the code that calls the function. When the chapter's program calls box_print('x', 1, 3) inside a try block, the exception raised for the width is caught by the except clause and the program prints An exception happened: Width must be greater than 2. A second call with the two-character symbol ZZ prints An exception happened: Symbol must be a single character string. (Sweigart, 2025). When Python executes raise, it stops the current function at that line and starts looking for an except clause that matches the exception, first in the function itself and then in each caller above it. A bare raise with no expression inside an except clause re-raises the exception that is being handled, so a handler can look at an error and then let it continue (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The statement raise ValueError is shorthand for raise ValueError(), which creates the exception without a message. A raise statement outside any try block does not give an error of its own; it ends the program with a traceback. And a raise inside a function does not return a value to the caller: the code after it in the same function never runs. Write the message so that someone who has not seen the code can act on it; Width must be greater than 2. says what was wrong and what is needed. slides.title: Exception class
slides.say: The class tells a handler what happened without parsing the message. ValueError is documented as raised when an operation or function receives an argument that has the right type but an inappropriate value; TypeError, NameError and ZeroDivisionError each name a different situation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that raises the most specific class lets its callers write except clauses that react to one problem and leave the others alone. The class name is the first word on the last line of every traceback, for example ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'. The chapter raises plain Exception objects with a message, which is the simplest form; the tutorial advises that programs that define their own exceptions derive them from the Exception class and give them names that end in Error (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An except clause names a class and catches every exception that is an instance of that class or of a subclass. The expression issubclass(ValueError, Exception) is True, so except Exception catches a ValueError, whereas except TypeError does not: a program that raises ValueError('bad value') inside a try block with only an except TypeError clause is not stopped there, and the exception is caught by an outer except ValueError clause that prints outer caught bad value. Catching Exception is the broadest ordinary choice and hides the difference between a mistake by the user and a mistake by the programmer, so prefer the narrowest class that fits. The most extreme classes, such as KeyboardInterrupt, are not subclasses of Exception: issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception) is False, so an except Exception clause does not catch a user's Control-C. slides.title: Exception message
slides.say: The message is the part of an error that a person reads. A program that prints a clear message when something goes wrong helps the user to correct the input, whereas a traceback shows only the programmer where the code was. The chapter uses the except Exception as err form for exactly this purpose: it stores the exception object in a variable named err and converts it to a string with str to produce a user-friendly error message (Sweigart, 2025). The form appears in the chapter's boxPrint.py: the except clause prints the text An exception happened: followed by str(err). The same form is the standard way to show or log an error without letting the program crash, and the message is the line that follows the class name in a traceback (Sweigart, 2025). Writing as err after the class in the except clause binds the exception that was caught to the name err for the length of the clause. The expression Exception('custom message').args evaluates to ('custom message',), a tuple with one item, and str(Exception('custom message')) evaluates to 'custom message'. An exception with two arguments is shown as a tuple, str(Exception('a', 'b')) being "('a', 'b')", and an exception created without arguments has an empty message. The message is for people and not for code. A handler that decides what to do by comparing the text of the message breaks as soon as the wording changes, so decide by the exception class and keep the message for display. Printing the exception object directly, print(err), shows the same text as print(str(err)), because print converts its arguments to strings (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Argument validation
slides.say: A function cannot trust its callers, and a user who typed something into a program is the least trustworthy caller of all. Validating at the start of the function keeps a bad value from travelling deeper into the program, where it would cause a failure far from its source. The chapter says that for errors a program can meet as a normal part of its operation, such as a file not being found or invalid data entered by the user, an exception should be raised and not detected with an assert statement (Sweigart, 2025). Validation is found at the top of almost every function that receives data from outside: a user, a file or another program. The Python glossary names two coding styles around this idea. Look before you leap tests the preconditions with if statements before acting; easier to ask for forgiveness than permission assumes that things are valid and catches the exception if not (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Validation with raise is the first style, and the try and except around a call is the second. A small function shows the pattern. After def area(width), the lines if width <= 0 and raise ValueError('width must be positive, got ' + str(width)) refuse the bad value before the function computes width * 2. A loop that calls area(3) and area(0) inside try prints 6 for the first call and refused: width must be positive, got 0 for the second. Do the validation before any effect of the function has happened, such as printing or changing data, so that a refused call leaves nothing half done. Put in the message the value that was received and the value that was expected. And do not validate with assert: an assert statement can be removed from a running program, and a check that must always happen belongs in an if with a raise.

slides.title: Unhandled exception
slides.say: Letting an exception go unhandled is often the right design. A programming error that the program cannot repair is better reported at once, with the traceback that shows its origin, than hidden. The Python tutorial observes that most exceptions are not handled by programs and result in error messages (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The situation is met whenever a program fails with a traceback in the terminal, and it is the usual fate of an AssertionError, which the chapter says should not be caught. The interpreter's hook for it is sys.excepthook: when an exception other than SystemExit is raised and uncaught, the interpreter calls this function with the exception class, the exception instance and the traceback, and it prints them to sys.stderr (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that prints before, raises Exception('boom') and then has a print of after shows exactly the behaviour. Only before reaches the screen, the traceback ends with the line Exception: boom, and the process finishes with the exit status 1. The statement after the raise never runs. Shells and other programs treat a nonzero exit status as abnormal termination (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A crash can leave work unfinished, such as a half-written result, so a program that must clean up needs a finally clause or a handler near the top. In the other direction, do not wrap the whole program in except Exception only to hide tracebacks: the traceback is the most useful clue that the program has. slides.title: Tracebacks
slides.say: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an exception is not handled. It lists the chain of function calls that led to the line where the exception was raised, ending with the class and the message of the exception. The Python tutorial calls the preceding part of the error message the context in which the exception occurred, in the form of a stack traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The traceback answers the question where the program was when it failed, and it answers it without running anything again. Reading it well is the most economical debugging skill: a learner who can read a traceback knows which file, which line and which call to look at first. The concepts that follow explain how an exception travels up the call stack, how the lines of a traceback are read, how Python 3.11 and later point at the failing part of a line, how notes add context while an exception is re-raised, and why the report appears on the error stream. slides.title: Exception unwinding
slides.say: Unwinding is what makes it possible to raise an exception in a deep helper function and handle it at the one place that knows what to do. The traceback is a record of the same journey, so understanding the unwinding is what makes a traceback readable: its lines are the functions that the exception left. A program with three small functions shows it. In it process calls load, load calls read_age, and read_age calls int on its text. Given the text 'abc', int raises a ValueError in read_age, no function on the way handles it, and it is caught by an except ValueError clause around the call to process in the main program, which prints caught: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'. The journey can be inspected, because the exception object keeps its traceback. Listing the function names of the traceback gives ['<module>', 'process', 'load', 'read_age'], from the outermost call to the one that raised. Without the handler, the same journey ends at the top of the program: Python prints the traceback, with these four entries, and the program ends with an exit status of 1. The handler can be anywhere along the way, and the nearer it is to the raise the less of the program is skipped. A handler placed too low may swallow an error that a caller wanted to see, while one placed too high may skip work that could have been done. Decide where the program can do something useful about the error, and handle it there. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Traceback reading
slides.say: The header says how the entries are arranged: the most recent call is last. The outermost call, usually the module itself, comes first, and the call that raised the exception comes last, just above the message. Because the cause of the exception is in the last entry and the reason it was reached is in the earlier ones, the reader usually starts at the bottom and works upwards. In the three-function program of the previous concept, a traceback of the unhandled error begins with the header, continues with the entry File "main.py", line 7, in <module>, and ends with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'. The names of the entries are <module>, process, load and read_age, with the line numbers 7, 6, 4 and 2, and the source line of the last entry is return int(text). The line number is where execution was inside that function when it called the next one, so each entry except the last points at a call. The last entry points at the line that raised. The header and the last line are the same in every recent version of Python, but the lines between them are refined from release to release, for example by the finer marks that the next concept describes. Reading from the top and stopping at the first entry is a common mistake. That entry is usually the main program calling something, and it is the last entry that shows where the problem happened. Note too that code typed directly into the interpreter or given with python -c has no file to read from, so such entries have no source line.

slides.title: Fine grained locations
slides.say: A single line can contain many operations. The PEP gives the case of x['a']['b']['c']['d'] = 1, where a TypeError that says 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable cannot tell which of the dictionaries was None, so users often had to attach a debugger or split up the expression (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). The marks answer the question directly. The marks appear in any traceback printed by the standard interpreter. A dictionary maps keys to values, and a subscript is the square-bracket lookup of a key. For data = {'a': {'b': None}}, the line print(data['a']['b']['c']) fails with TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, and the carets lie under the last subscript, ['c'], while tildes run under data['a']['b'], the value that was None. Python records, for each bytecode instruction, the start and end columns of the source it came from, and the traceback machinery uses these ranges to draw the marks (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). The marks depend on the interpreter: for the call line process('abc') of the previous concept, Python 3.14 draws tildes and carets and Python 3.12 does not, so the exact picture varies between versions even when the first and last lines are the same. The marks can be switched off. The PEP provides the environment variable PYTHONNODEBUGRANGES and the option -X no_debug_ranges for those who want smaller files or a traceback in the old form (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). A program that parses traceback text should therefore not rely on the marks being present.

slides.title: Exception notes
slides.say: A message is written where the exception is raised, but the useful context is often known only further up, for example which record or which field was being processed. Notes allow the code that catches the exception to add this information and re-raise the same exception, without hiding the original class or traceback behind a new exception. The pattern is used when a handler cannot repair a problem but knows more than the raiser. The Python tutorial shows a handler that adds a note and then uses a bare raise, so the traceback ends with the exception and its notes in the order they were added (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a program that tries int('abc'), catches the ValueError, calls add_note('while reading the age field') and then raises again, the last two lines of the traceback are ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc' and while reading the age field. The attribute __notes__ is created when add_note is first called, and the example panel of this page uses a one-line unnamed function, called a lambda, only to fit the call and the reading of __notes__ into one expression. The argument must be a string; passing anything else raises TypeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Notes are not part of the message, so str(err) does not contain them, and code that logs only str(err) loses them. Notes do not exist in versions before 3.11, so a program that must run on an older interpreter cannot call add_note. slides.title: Standard error stream
slides.say: Two channels let a program separate its results from its complaints. The results can be saved or passed on to another program while the error messages remain visible to the person at the terminal. A traceback is therefore never mixed into the normal output. In a terminal both streams are shown on the same screen, so the difference is easy to miss, but a program that captures the output of another sees it. In a test where a program prints one line normally and one line with print(..., file=sys.stderr), the standard output holds only to stdout and the standard error holds only to stderr. The standard logging handler also writes to sys.stderr when no other stream is given (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The function print writes to sys.stdout unless the keyword argument file is given, and an uncaught exception is reported by sys.excepthook, which prints the traceback to sys.stderr (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Writing to the error stream on purpose therefore needs only print(..., file=sys.stderr), where sys is the module that holds the streams. Do not print the information that other programs must read to the error stream, and do not print error messages to the standard output of a program whose output is processed further. Remember, too, that a log message sent to the screen goes by default to the error stream, not to the standard output.

slides.title: Assertion
slides.say: An assertion is a statement that a certain condition must be true at a certain point of a program, together with a check that stops the program at once if it is not. The chapter calls an assertion a sanity check, a test that makes sure the code is not doing something obviously wrong, and it performs such checks with the assert statement, which raises an AssertionError exception when the check fails (Sweigart, 2025). Assertions catch bugs close to their cause. The chapter recommends failing fast: a program that stops the moment a necessary condition is violated shortens the time between the original cause of the bug and the moment the programmer first notices it, and so reduces the amount of code to check (Sweigart, 2025). A wrong value that is allowed to travel through the program causes a failure far from its source. Assertions are written by the programmer, for the programmer. They appear at the boundaries inside a program: after a computation whose result has a known property, before using a value that earlier code was supposed to prepare, and at the end of a function whose contract can be stated in a line. The chapter limits them to programmer errors and keeps user errors for exceptions (Sweigart, 2025). This branch explains the assert statement with its form, its optional message and its failure, then the check that the chapter uses as its example, the difference between assertions and raised exceptions, and finally the optimised mode in which Python removes assertions altogether, which is the chapter's rule restated as a fact about the interpreter. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Assert
slides.say: The assert group covers the mechanics and the discipline of assertions. The mechanics are the statement, the check it performs, the error it raises and the message it can carry. The discipline is the knowledge of what an assertion may check and what it must not. Assertions are easy to write and easy to misuse. The same statement that gives an early warning during development can become a security or correctness hole if it stands in for a check that must always run, because Python can be told to leave assertions out. The concepts of this group therefore pair every mechanism with the limit that goes with it. The concepts begin with the idea of the sanity check and the statement that implements it, then the list example from the chapter, the failure, the message, the rule of fail fast, the choice between assertion and exception, the option that removes assertions, and the command-line options in general. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Sanity check
slides.say: The value of a sanity check lies in its cost and its timing. It costs one line and little running time, and it runs at the very point where the assumption is made, so a violation is reported there and not three functions later. The chapter's own example checks that after a list has been sorted its first item is not larger than its last (Sweigart, 2025). Typical sanity checks compare a computed total with the sum of its parts, check that a result has the expected length, check that a number lies within its allowed range, or check that a collection that should be sorted is in order. They are placed directly after the code whose result they test. The check is a condition, an expression whose value is True or False, and the assert statement stops the program when it is false. For example, sorted([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3] evaluates to True, so the check passes in silence, whereas sorted([3, 1, 2]) == [3, 2, 1] evaluates to False and an assertion built from it would fail. A sanity check should be independent of the code it checks. If it recomputes the result with the same faulty logic, it will agree with the bug. And a check that is wrong itself, for example a comparison with the wrong operator, produces false alarms that teach the programmer to ignore assertions. slides.title: Assert statement
slides.say: The statement turns a belief into a check. A programmer who writes assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] records a belief about the list, and the interpreter verifies it every time the line runs. If the belief becomes false, because of a later change or an input that was not foreseen, the statement reports it at once. The statement is used in programs, in functions, and in the interactive shell, as the chapter does when it enters assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] after sorting a list (Sweigart, 2025). The Python language reference introduces assert statements as a convenient way to insert debugging assertions into a program (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The language reference defines the simple form, assert expression, as equivalent to if __debug__: followed by if not expression: raise AssertionError, and the form with a message as the same with raise AssertionError(expression2) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The special name __debug__ is normally True, so the check runs. When the condition is true the statement does nothing at all, and the program continues with the next line. Do not put the condition and the message in parentheses together. The statement assert (False, 'msg') tests a tuple with two items, and a tuple that is not empty counts as true, so the check can never fail; Python warns about it with a SyntaxWarning that says assertion is always true, perhaps remove parentheses? (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Also avoid conditions that change something, because under optimisation the condition is not evaluated at all. slides.title: Sorted-order check
slides.say: The example shows how a single assert guards a whole step of work. If the list has really been sorted from smallest to largest, then the first item cannot be larger than the last. If the check fails, something other than sorting has happened to the list, which is the kind of bug that would otherwise show up much later as a strange result. In the chapter the list is ages = [26, 57, 92, 54, 22, 15, 17, 80, 47, 73]. The method sort() puts the items in ascending order in place, giving [15, 17, 22, 26, 47, 54, 57, 73, 80, 92], and the assertion passes. The method reverse() reverses the list in place, giving [73, 47, 80, 17, 15, 22, 54, 92, 57, 26], and the same assertion raises an AssertionError (Sweigart, 2025). Both sort() and reverse() change the list in place, which is why the chapter calls them in separate statements and then looks at the list (Python Software Foundation, 2026); when they are run they give back None, so a line such as ages = ages.sort() would destroy the list. The comparison ages[0] <= ages[-1] is True for the sorted list, because 15 <= 92, and False for the reversed one, because 73 <= 26 is false. The example panel of this page uses a one-line unnamed function, a lambda, only to sort a list and compare in one expression. The check is deliberately weak. A list in which the first item happens to be smaller than the last passes the assertion even though the list is not sorted, as [1, 3, 2] does. A stronger check compares every neighbouring pair, or compares the list with sorted(list). Choose a check strong enough for the risk, and remember that it protects only against the mistake it names. slides.title: Assertion failure
slides.say: What distinguishes it is how the chapter wants it treated. Unlike other exceptions, assert statements should not be handled with try and except; if an assert fails, the program should crash (Sweigart, 2025). The failure means that the programmer's model of the program is wrong, and a handler that continues with a wrong model only postpones the damage. A failure shows up as a traceback whose last line is AssertionError, followed by the message if the assert had one. In the chapter's example the line assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] fails on the reversed list, and the traceback ends with AssertionError and nothing after it, because no message was given (Sweigart, 2025). In current Python the traceback also marks the whole condition under the failing line. Because no message was given, the exception's text is empty: str(AssertionError()) is the empty string. Because the class derives from Exception, issubclass(AssertionError, Exception) evaluates to True, so an except Exception clause would catch it, and that is exactly what the advice warns against. An unhandled failure ends the program with exit status 1, like any other unhandled exception. Never catch AssertionError to keep a program going. If a check is needed for input that comes from outside the program, the right tool is an if statement that raises a more specific exception such as ValueError, which a caller can reasonably handle. slides.title: Assert message
slides.say: A message tells the reader what the failed condition meant in the vocabulary of the program. The language reference remarks that it is unnecessary to include the source code of the failed expression in the message, since it is displayed as part of the stack trace, so the message is best used for the values that the source cannot show (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A message is useful when the same assertion could fail for several reasons or when the values matter. A common form builds the message with an f-string, for example assert x > 0, f'x must be positive, got {x}', which for x equal to -1 gives the message x must be positive, got -1. The second expression is evaluated only when the condition is false (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that prints msg evaluated before returning the text bad and is used as the message does not run when the condition is true, and the program continues; when the condition is false it runs once and the error text is bad. This is why a message can safely contain a call that would be wasteful to execute on every pass. Keep the message free of side effects, since it runs only on failure and would make the failing run behave differently from a passing one. And keep it short and factual: the text goes to the programmer, not to the user, and a user should never see it. slides.title: Fail fast
slides.say: The distance between cause and symptom is what makes bugs expensive. A negative value that enters a calculation may produce a wrong total that is printed pages later. If the program had stopped at the negative value, the cause would have been on the line in the traceback. The principle is applied wherever a check can be placed cheaply near the assumption: at the start of a function, after an input has been converted, and after a step whose result is known to have a property. The chapter summarises that assertions are only for errors the program should not try to recover from, and that they should fail fast; otherwise an exception should be raised (Sweigart, 2025). A program that does not fail fast continues to run with bad data, and the damage grows with every step. A program that does fail fast raises the exception at once, Python prints a traceback that names the file and line of the check, and the search for the cause starts there. The assert statement is the simplest implementation of the idea, and the raise statement is the more general one. Failing fast belongs in development and in code where an error is a bug. For a service that must keep running or a program with a user at the keyboard, the same moment of detection should lead to a handled exception or a clear message, and not to a crash that destroys the user's work.

slides.title: Assert versus raise
slides.say: The difference matters because the two have different audiences and different guarantees. An exception is part of the program's behaviour and the user may see its message. An assertion should fail only while the program is under development, and a user should never see an assertion error in a finished program (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference adds a technical difference: assert is equivalent to raising AssertionError only when __debug__ is true, so an assertion may not run at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that sets an age shows the choice. If the age comes from a form that a person filled in, a negative value is a user error, and the function checks it with if age < 0 and raises ValueError. If the age was computed by earlier code that is supposed to return only non-negative values, a negative age means that the program itself is wrong, and an assert age >= 0 expresses that belief. A practical test is to ask who could cause the condition to be false. If a user, a file, a network or another program could, then the check must always run and must lead to a recoverable error, so it is an if with a raise. If only a mistake in the program itself could, then it is an assertion. Because assertions can be removed by an option of the interpreter, only the second kind may rely on them. The boundary moves. A function that is called only from the program's own code may use an assertion for its argument, and the same function offered to other programmers as a library must validate its arguments with exceptions, because strangers do not follow the program's own rules.

slides.title: Optimised mode
slides.say: The mode explains the chapter's rule that assertions are for programmer errors. A program that depends on an assertion for correct behaviour would behave differently when run with -O, so assertions must never carry a check that the program needs for its own safety, such as validation of what a user typed. The mode is met when a program is run with optimisation in real use, when the environment variable PYTHONOPTIMIZE is set, and when code is compiled by hand. The function compile takes an optimize level in which 0 means no optimisation and __debug__ is true, 1 means that asserts are removed and __debug__ is false, and 2 removes docstrings too, that is the string literals that appear as the first expression of a function, class or module (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The statement assert False normally raises AssertionError. A program that runs assert False and then prints reached prints nothing on the screen but a traceback in a normal run, and prints reached when it is started with python -O. In the same way __debug__ is True in a normal run and False under -O, and compiling a source string with optimize=1 and executing it reaches the line after the assert. The compiler, the part of Python that turns source code into bytecode, emits no code for an assert statement when optimisation is requested, so even a condition with a side effect is not evaluated (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Test a program that is meant to run with -O under that option as well. Assignments to __debug__ are illegal, so a program cannot switch its assertions on or off by itself. slides.title: Command-line option
slides.say: Options let one installation of Python behave in several ways without changing any program. This chapter uses three of them: -O, which removes assertions, -c, which runs the statements given on the command line, and -m, which runs a module as a script, as in python -m pdb. A learner who knows the options can read the documentation of the interpreter and of the tools that go with it. Options are typed in a terminal after the name of the interpreter. A running program can find out which of them are in force: the value sys.flags reports them, and its optimize field stands for -O or -OO, so it is 0 in a normal run and 1 under -O (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The interpreter reads the options first and then the program. An interface option such as -c or -m ends the list of options that the interpreter itself consumes, and the arguments after it end up in sys.argv, where the program or the module run with -m reads them (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That is why, in python -m pdb -p, the -p belongs to the debugger and not to the interpreter. For example, python -O -c "print(__debug__)" prints False, and python -c "print(__debug__)" prints True. Options and environment variables overlap: the documentation notes that it is customary for command-line switches to override environment variables where there is a conflict (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because several versions of Python may be installed side by side, check which interpreter and which options a script is actually run with when its behaviour surprises you. slides.title: Logging
slides.say: Logging is the practice of making a program write down what it does while it runs. The Python logging HOWTO defines it as a means of tracking events that happen when some software runs: the developer adds logging calls to the code to indicate that certain events have occurred, and each event is described by a message and has an importance, which is called its level or severity (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter introduces the logging module as a way to create a record of custom messages that describes when execution reached a call and which values the variables held (Sweigart, 2025). Logging gives the programmer a trail of breadcrumbs that can help to work out when things started to go wrong, and a missing message tells equally clearly that a part of the code was skipped (Sweigart, 2025). Unlike a bare print call, a log message has a level, a time and a destination, and all of them can be changed without editing the lines that produce the messages. That makes it possible to leave the calls in a finished program and still silence them. Logging is met in the chapter's factorial program, in the terminal output of nearly every large Python tool and in the log files of servers. The logging module is part of the standard library, so a program needs only to import it. The same module serves a three-line script and a large application, by the same four ideas: a logger that receives the calls, a handler that decides where a message goes, a level that decides which messages count, and a format that decides how a message looks. This branch has four parts. Setup explains the call that configures the system, the format, the destination and the rule by which a second configuration is ignored. Loggers and handlers explains the objects behind the simple calls. Levels explains the five levels, the threshold, the default and the way of switching everything off. Practice explains why logging is better than print and how to write the calls well. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Setup
slides.say: Setting up logging means telling the module three things: which messages count, how a message should look and where it should go. The chapter does all three with one call placed at the top of the program, logging.basicConfig, with the arguments level, format and, optionally, filename (Sweigart, 2025). Without a setup a program prints only warnings and worse, in a fixed shape, to the error stream. The setup is what turns logging into a debugging tool for the programmer: lowering the threshold to DEBUG shows everything, and a format with a time shows the order and the pace of events. The concepts of this group follow the order of the arguments. basicConfig itself comes first, then the format string and the percent placeholders it is written with, then the log file, and then the rule that makes a second call of basicConfig do nothing unless it is forced. slides.title: Basic config
slides.say: The call is the shortest path from no logging to useful logging. It makes the standard messages visible and gives them a layout, and the programmer does not have to learn about loggers and handlers first. The HOWTO says that for simple usage a format with the level name, the message and perhaps the time of the event is all that is needed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The call is placed once, near the top of the main program, before any message is logged. The HOWTO states that the call should come before any calls to a logger's methods such as debug() and info(), otherwise that logging event may not be handled in the desired manner (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the chapter it stands under the import of the logging module in factorialLog.py. A program that calls logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(levelname)s - %(message)s') and then logs a debug message and an info message prints DEBUG - Start of program and INFO - going on, on the error stream. The functions debug, info, warning, error and critical call basicConfig automatically if no handlers are defined for the root logger (Python Software Foundation, 2026), which is why the chapter's description of debug() as calling basicConfig is true only when the program has not configured logging itself. The call can be silently ignored. It does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, which includes the case where an earlier logging call has configured the system implicitly, and a later concept shows the effect. Also, basicConfig must be called from the main thread before other threads are started (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Keep it at the very top of the program. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Log format
slides.say: The format decides how useful a log is when read later. The time shows how long a step took, the level shows how serious the line is, and the message says what happened. A format that adds the function name or the line number lets the reader find the call that produced a line. The format string is passed to basicConfig as the format argument. The library reference lists the fields of a log record that can be used: asctime is the human-readable time at which the record was created, of the form 2003-07-08 16:49:45,896 where the digits after the comma are milliseconds; levelname is the text of the level; message is the logged message; and others such as funcName and lineno name the place of the call (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When no format is given, basicConfig uses the default, which has the attributes levelname, name and message separated by colons (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so logging.warning('Watch out!') prints WARNING:root:Watch out!. With the format '%(levelname)s - %(message)s' the same record is shown as WARNING - Watch out!. The chapter's printed times, such as 2035-05-23 16:20:12,664, are illustrations; a real run prints the clock time of the machine, in the same shape. A field name that is not an attribute of the record does not stop the program. The logging package is designed to swallow exceptions that occur while logging, so for the format '%(nofield)s' the first message produces a --- Logging error --- report with a traceback on the error stream, ending in ValueError: Formatting field not found in record: 'nofield', and the program carries on (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Write the field list carefully, with the letter s that follows each closing parenthesis. The style argument of basicConfig lets a format use braces or dollar signs instead of percent signs, but the percent style is the default and the one the chapter uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Percent placeholder
slides.say: The logging module is older than formatted string literals, and the logging HOWTO explains that merging variable data into a message uses this old, percent style for backwards compatibility (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A learner who meets logging.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total) in real code needs to read the markers, and the log format string of basicConfig is written in the same notation. The markers appear in two places in logging: in the message of a log call, where each marker is filled from the arguments that follow the message, and in the format string, where a marker with a name in parentheses, such as %(levelname)s, is filled from the attributes of the log record. The second form is the one that takes its values from a dictionary, which maps names to values; the reference shows '%(language)s has %(number)03d quote types.' filled with a dictionary, giving 'Python has 002 quote types.' (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Python scans the string for markers and fills them in order from a tuple, or by name from a dictionary. The count must fit: '%s %s' % ('a',) raises a TypeError with the message not enough arguments for format string, and '%s' % (1, 2) raises one with not all arguments converted during string formatting. The logging module avoids both at the call: it merges the message and the arguments only when a record is emitted, and a message given no arguments is not formatted at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A literal percent sign in a message that has arguments must be written as %%, because a lone one starts a conversion. The reference itself notes that the operations have quirks that lead to common errors, and recommends formatted string literals, str.format() or string.Template as alternatives for ordinary text (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In ordinary code use an f-string; in the arguments of a log call use the markers. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Log to file
slides.say: Messages on the screen clutter the output of the program and disappear when the window is closed. Written to a file, they keep the screen clear and can be read after the program has run, as the chapter points out (Sweigart, 2025). A file is also the only practical place for the log of a program that runs without anyone watching it. The option is used when a program runs unattended or writes more messages than anyone would read on a screen, and the file is read afterwards with an editor or a program. The library reference explains the mechanism: specifying filename makes basicConfig create a FileHandler with that name, rather than a StreamHandler (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The file is opened in the mode given by filemode, which defaults to 'a' (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and the HOWTO explains the result: if the script is run several times, the messages of successive runs are appended to the file, and a filemode of 'w' makes every run start afresh (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a test in which a short program is run twice with the same file name, the file holds two lines DEBUG - run; run twice again with filemode='w', it holds one. By default the file grows indefinitely, as the FileHandler documentation warns (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so a long-lived program needs a plan for old logs. The HOWTO's file example also passes encoding='utf-8', so that text such as Malmö is written correctly; the glossary explains that a string has to be serialized as a sequence of bytes to be stored, and the text encoding is the rule for that (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And an argument conflict is an error: the library reference says that stream is incompatible with filename, and that giving both raises a ValueError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Force reconfigure
slides.say: The rule is a frequent source of confusion, because the second call fails silently. A learner who changes the level in a program, or experiments in an interactive session, sees no effect and no error. Knowing the rule, and the one-word remedy, saves a lot of puzzling. It is met in the interactive shell, where earlier lines have already configured logging, in test suites, and in programs in which a library configures logging before the main program does. The chapter does not mention the rule. A program that calls basicConfig with level WARNING and the format 'first %(message)s', then again with level DEBUG and the format 'second %(message)s', and then logs a debug and a warning message prints only first w, because the second call is ignored. After a third call with force=True and the format 'third %(message)s', a debug message prints third d2. An implicit configuration counts too. The call logging.warning('first') configures the root logger by itself, because it has no handlers, and a later basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is then ignored: a following logging.debug call prints nothing and the level of the root logger is still 30. Place basicConfig before any other logging call, or use force=True when the order cannot be controlled. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Loggers and handlers
slides.say: Behind the simple module-level functions of logging stands a small system of objects. The Python documentation says that the library takes a modular approach and offers several categories of components: loggers expose the interface that application code uses, handlers send the log records to the right destination, filters decide finer which records to output, and formatters specify the layout of the final output (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The system explains behaviour that the one-line setup hides: why a message from one part of a program can be shown while another is not, why a message can appear twice, and why basicConfig can be ignored. A learner who knows the logger, the handler and the record can read the documentation of logging and the logs of larger programs. The concepts of this group are the logger, which receives the calls and chooses by level, the handler, which delivers the record to a destination, and the log record, the object that carries the details of one event from the first to the second. Log information is passed between loggers, handlers, filters and formatters in a LogRecord instance (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Logger
slides.say: Loggers let the parts of a large program log separately. A name such as the one a module has, which the documentation recommends for the purpose, tells the reader where a message came from, and the threshold of one logger can be changed without touching the others. A library written by someone else can log through its own logger and leave the choices to the application (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the chapter a logger is present but not named: the functions logging.debug, logging.info, logging.warning, logging.error and logging.critical just call the same-named method of the root logger, whose name is printed as root in the output (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Larger programs write logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top of each module, where __name__ is the module's name. In a check, the call logging.getLogger() returns an object of the class RootLogger whose name is 'root', logging.getLogger('app') is logging.getLogger('app') is True, and once the logger 'app' exists the parent of logging.getLogger('app.db') is the logger named 'app'. A new logger has no level of its own, so its effective level is that of its nearest ancestor with one; for 'app.db' that is the root's level, 30, unless something sets another (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation says that loggers should never be created directly but always through the function getLogger (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A message from a named logger is also handled differently when nothing is configured: it is printed as the bare message by the handler of last resort, instead of in the root format. Do not log to the root logger in a library, so that the application can configure it as it likes (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Handler
slides.say: Handlers separate what is logged from where it goes. The same record can be sent to the screen and to a file, each with its own format and threshold, without changing the line that logs it. This separation is what makes it possible to change the destination of a whole program by changing its setup only. In the chapter handlers are created for the reader by basicConfig. Without a filename it makes a StreamHandler, and with filename it makes a FileHandler (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The list of the handlers of the root logger is available as logging.getLogger().handlers: it is the empty list in a program that has not logged anything, and after logging.basicConfig() it holds one handler of the class StreamHandler. When a logger accepts a call, it creates a record and offers it to its handlers, and then, if its propagate attribute is true, to the handlers of its parent loggers. If no handler is found in the whole chain, the handler of last resort is used, a StreamHandler writing to sys.stderr with the level WARNING (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That explains why a warning from an unconfigured named logger still appears on the screen while its info messages do not. Do not attach the same handler to a logger and to its ancestors: the documentation warns that a record may then be emitted several times (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reason why basicConfig does nothing on a second call is that it checks whether the root logger already has handlers.

slides.title: Log record
slides.say: The record is the common currency of the logging system. Loggers, handlers, filters and formatters all work on records, and the fields of the record are the names that a format string can use. Knowing what a record holds shows what a log line can contain. A record is never seen in the simple use of the chapter, but its attributes are what the format string selects: asctime, levelname and message are all attributes of the record (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The attribute levelname is the text of the level, 'INFO' for 20, and levelno is the number. The message of a record is computed as msg % args when it is needed. With msg equal to 'hello %s' and args equal to ('world',), the call getMessage() returns 'hello world', and the record created for a level of 20 has the levelname 'INFO'. If a message is given without arguments, no percent formatting is done, so the message '100%' is returned as it is (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The record is created only if the logger is enabled for the level of the call, so a call below the threshold is cheap: in a test that counts how many records are created, a debug call to a logger whose threshold is WARNING creates none and a warning call creates one. The formatted message and the time are computed later, when the record is handled. Arbitrary objects can also be used as the message, in which case str is called on them to produce the text (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Levels
slides.say: Levels are the importance ranks that log messages carry. There are five of them, from the least to the most important, and each has a name, a number and a function of the same name. The chapter describes them in Table 5-1 and explains that logging levels provide a way to categorise log messages by importance, so that less important messages can be filtered out while testing (Sweigart, 2025). The levels allow one program to produce a lot of output while it is being developed and little when it is finished, without changing any logging call. The programmer decides the level of each message once, and the setup decides which levels are shown. This turns logging into a dial that can be turned from detailed to silent. The group has four concepts: the five levels and their numbers, the threshold that selects among them, the default threshold that applies when nothing has been configured, and logging.disable, which silences levels from outside the program's own setup. slides.title: Logging levels
slides.say: A level states how much attention a message deserves. The chapter explains them in its Table 5-1: DEBUG is the lowest level, used for small details that matter only when diagnosing problems; INFO records general events or confirms that the program works; WARNING indicates a potential problem that does not yet stop the program; ERROR records an error that made the program fail to do something; and CRITICAL is the highest level, for a fatal error that has caused, or is about to cause, the program to stop (Sweigart, 2025). Each level is used by calling the function with the same name as the level in lower case. A program that sets the level to DEBUG with format '%(levelname)s - %(message)s' and logs one message at each level prints DEBUG - d, INFO - i, WARNING - w, ERROR - e and CRITICAL - c, in the order of the calls. The numbers make the comparison of importance possible: a message is accepted if its number is not lower than the threshold. The module defines the five names as constants, so logging.DEBUG is the number 10 and logging.CRITICAL is 50. Levels of one's own can be defined with logging.addLevelName, but all levels used must be registered with it, and the documentation calls a custom level higher than CRITICAL not recommended (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The level of a message is the programmer's judgment, not a property that Python can check: as the chapter says, it is up to you to decide which category your log message falls into (Sweigart, 2025). Do not use CRITICAL for routine trouble, since a level that is used for everything no longer separates anything. slides.title: Level threshold
slides.say: The threshold is the dial of the chapter's logging system. During development it is DEBUG, which the chapter says shows messages from all the logging levels. Later, when the programmer is interested only in errors, level=logging.ERROR shows only ERROR and CRITICAL messages and skips the DEBUG, INFO and WARNING messages (Sweigart, 2025). It is set once, in the setup of the program, and often read from a setting so that a user can ask for more detail without editing the program. The HOWTO shows how to turn a command-line option such as --log=INFO into the number to pass as level, with getattr(logging, loglevel.upper()) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a program that sets level=logging.ERROR and logs one message at each level, only ERROR - e and CRITICAL - c appear. The comparison uses the numbers: 40 and 50 are not lower than the threshold 40, whereas 10, 20 and 30 are. Nothing is deleted or changed in the logging calls; changing the one word in the setup brings the other messages back. There are two thresholds, one in the logger and one in each handler, and a message must pass both. The logger's level is checked first; a handler with a higher level of its own will drop the record afterwards. If a message does not appear although the logger's level is low enough, look at the level of the handler.

slides.title: Default level
slides.say: The default explains a very common surprise. A learner writes logging.debug('value is 3') and sees nothing, because debug messages are below the default threshold. The chapter avoids the surprise by always calling basicConfig with level=logging.DEBUG first (Sweigart, 2025). The default is met in any program that imports logging and logs without a setup, in the interactive shell, and in code that libraries run. In such a program logging.warning('Watch out!') prints WARNING:root:Watch out!, and logging.info('I told you so') prints nothing, as the HOWTO shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The expression logging.getLogger().getEffectiveLevel() evaluates to 30 in a fresh program, the number of WARNING. The functions logging.warning and logging.error find no handler on the root logger, and so they call basicConfig themselves, with the default format, to the error stream; a program that calls logging.warning('w') and logging.error('e') prints WARNING:root:w and ERROR:root:e. A named logger that has no configuration at all is served by the handler of last resort, which prints the bare message, such as bare, for WARNING and above (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The side effect on the root logger is the trap: after the first implicit call the root logger has a handler, so a later basicConfig is ignored. Debug messages that are missing from the output are therefore explained by the default threshold or by an earlier implicit configuration, and the fix is level=logging.DEBUG in a first call of basicConfig or force=True. slides.title: Disabling logging
slides.say: A finished program should not fill the screen with debugging messages, and deleting the calls would make the next debugging session start from nothing. A single line that can be commented out or in turns all the messages on and off. The chapter advises putting it near the import logging line so that it is easy to find (Sweigart, 2025). It is used at the end of development, in tests that should run quietly, and in a program that wants a global quiet switch. Called with no argument, it uses the level CRITICAL, which is the default since Python 3.7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a program that sets level=logging.INFO, logs a critical message, calls logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) and logs again, the first message appears as CRITICAL - before and the later critical and error messages are silent. Calling logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) removes the override, so a following error message appears as ERROR - after. A call with logging.INFO discards INFO and DEBUG events only, so a later warning still prints. The disable level applies to all loggers in the process, including those of libraries, and it overrides their own settings, so a program that disables logging for a test must undo it. The setting is a number: logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) is the way back, not logging.enable, which does not exist.
