slides.title: Practice
slides.say: Practice in logging is the set of habits that decide whether log messages help or hinder. The first habit is to choose logging and not print for the diagnostic output of a program, and the second is to write the log calls so that they cost little when the messages are not wanted. A log that is easy to switch off, and cheap when off, is a log the programmer will leave in the program. A log full of expensive string building is one that has to be removed before the program is released, which brings back the problem that logging was meant to solve. The two concepts are the comparison of logging with print, which the chapter makes in its section A Poor Practice and in its practice questions, and the lazy formatting of messages, which the logging documentation explains. slides.title: Logging versus print
slides.say: The chapter calls debugging with print a poor practice. When the debugging is done, the programmer has to remove each print call, and may accidentally remove calls that were used for non-log messages. With logging, a program may be filled with as many messages as the programmer likes and all of them can be disabled later with one logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) call (Sweigart, 2025). The Python logging HOWTO sets the same division in a table: to display console output for the ordinary usage of a command line script or program, use print; to report events that occur during normal operation, such as for status monitoring or fault investigation, use a logger's info or debug method (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Each log call also adds a level and, if the format asks for it, a time, and it goes by default to the error stream, whereas print goes to the standard output. A program that prints one line with print and logs one line with logging.warning shows both until logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) is called; after it only the print line remains. The distinction is easy to blur in small scripts: a message the user needs, such as the result of the calculation, must be printed, and must not depend on the logging setup, or it would vanish when logging is disabled. The chapter's factorial program makes the point: print(factorial(5)) is part of the original program, so the code displays the result even if logging messages are disabled (Sweigart, 2025).

slides.title: Lazy formatting
slides.say: Building a message can be costly, for example when an object has a long text form, and a program that logs inside a loop may build thousands of messages that no one will read. With deferred formatting a disabled debug call costs little more than the call itself, which makes it affordable to leave such calls in a finished program. The form is common in the code of libraries and of larger applications, which pass the values after the message as in log.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total). The percent markers are the ones explained under percent placeholders. A small experiment shows the difference. A class is a recipe for objects, and the method __str__ is what Python calls to turn an object into text; here it counts its calls. With the level at INFO, log.debug('value is %s', obj) leaves the count at 0, log.debug(f'value is {obj}') raises it to 1 although nothing is printed, and log.info('value is %s', obj) raises it to 2 and prints INFO:demo:value is noisy. Lazy formatting defers only the formatting. The arguments themselves are evaluated before the call, so an expensive function call among them still runs. The HOWTO's advice is to guard such a call with if logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG), so that the expensive functions are never called when the logger's threshold is above DEBUG (Python Software Foundation, 2026). slides.title: Debugger
slides.say: The debugger is a tool that runs a program one instruction at a time and lets the programmer look at the program between the steps. The chapter defines it as a feature of the Mu editor that executes a program one instruction at a time, giving a chance to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). A program started this way is said to run under the debugger. The same idea is offered by IDLE, by other editor software, and by the module pdb, the Python debugger, which ships with Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The debugger shows what a program actually does instead of what its author thinks it does. The chapter admits that the process is much slower than running the program at full speed, but it lets the programmer see the actual values in a program while it runs, rather than deduce what the values might be from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Exceptions, assertions and logging must be written into the program before it runs, and a question that the programmer did not think of in advance cannot be answered by them. The debugger can be started without changing the program, and then any variable can be read at any point. The chapter teaches the debugger inside the Mu editor, with buttons and a pane at the side of the window. The same tool is found in IDLE, whose documentation lists a debugger with persistent breakpoints and stepping among its features, and in the module pdb, which is part of the standard library and is controlled by typing short commands at a prompt (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in function breakpoint() lets a program start the debugger by itself at a chosen line, and since Python 3.14 pdb can also attach to a program that is already running. The branch has three groups. The first, the debugger interface, describes what the person sees: the editor, the act of running under the debugger, the pane that lists the variables, and the button that stops the session. The second, the controls, describes how the person moves through the program: breakpoints, Continue, Step In, Step Over and Step Out. The third, the Python debugger, shows the same controls as commands of pdb and explains breakpoint(), the environment variable that configures it, and attaching to a running process. The debugger shows only the values that the program has at the moment it is paused. It does not remember how the values got there, so a bug whose cause lies far back in the run can still require several sessions or a log. The chapter also reminds the reader that a program that waits for typed input still waits under the debugger (Sweigart, 2025). Finally, the debugger is a convenience of the editor or of pdb and not a feature of the language, so the buttons and wording of one tool do not carry over unchanged to another. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Debugger interface
slides.say: The debugger interface is everything the person at the keyboard sees and touches while a program runs under the debugger. The chapter describes it for the Mu editor: the editor window in which the debugger is started, the Debug button that starts it, the Debug Inspector pane that lists the values of the variables, and the Stop button that ends the session (Sweigart, 2025). These four parts are the subject of the concepts in this group. The same four parts exist in every debugger, even though their look differs. IDLE starts its debugger from a toggle in a menu and marks breakpoints through a context menu (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and pdb replaces buttons and panes with commands typed at a prompt and answers printed as text. A student who knows what each part is for can therefore use whichever tool is at hand, and can read a transcript of a debugging session without having the window in front of them. The concepts follow the order of a debugging session: the editor in which it takes place, running a program under the debugger so that it pauses before its first line, reading the program state in the inspector pane, and stopping the program. The controls that move the program forward, namely breakpoints, Continue and the three kinds of step, belong to the next group. Because the windows of Mu cannot be reproduced in text, the transcripts quoted in this group were produced by running pdb on the same kind of program. slides.title: Mu editor
slides.say: A named editor gives the instructions of the chapter something to refer to. The chapter's instructions say to click a button or to click a line number, and they are only understandable if the reader knows which window and which button are meant. The editor is also where the program's text, its output and its debugger meet: the program is edited in the file editor, a running program writes into the output pane, and, as the chapter notes, a program that calls input() waits for the answer to be typed into that output pane (Sweigart, 2025). The window of Mu appears in the figures of the chapter. Figure 5-1 shows the program paused before its first line, with that line highlighted in the file editor, and Figure 5-3 shows the pane at the right with the variables of the adding program (Sweigart, 2025). Other editors offer the same facilities under other names. The IDLE page of the Python documentation, for example, describes a Debugger entry that makes code entered in the Shell or run from an Editor run under the debugger, and IDLE is described in the glossary as an editor and interpreter environment that ships with the standard distribution of Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Starting the debugger in Mu is a matter of clicking Debug instead of Run. The Debug Inspector pane then opens at the right side of the window, and Debugging mode adds the buttons Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out to the top of the editor, next to the usual Stop button (Sweigart, 2025). Everything else, editing the text and saving the file, works as before. The same program can therefore be run in the two ways one after the other, which is how the chapter proceeds with its adding program. Mu is one editor among many, and its buttons and menus are not part of Python. The chapter itself remarks that Mu should prevent the debugger from entering Python's built-in functions (Sweigart, 2025), a convenience that a command-line debugger does not necessarily share. The IDLE documentation warns that its debugger is still incomplete and somewhat experimental (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When a button named in the chapter is not found in another editor, the underlying idea, pause, look, step, continue, is what to search for.

slides.title: Running under the debugger
slides.say: A normal run gives no chance to look inside: the program starts, prints its output and ends, and the programmer sees only the result. Under the debugger the programmer gets control before the first line and after every step, which is the only way to watch a variable change from line to line. The price, in the chapter's words, is speed: the process is much slower than running the program at full speed (Sweigart, 2025). The mode is therefore used on a program that is already known to misbehave, such as the adding program that prints 5342. The command-line debugger is started with the command python -m pdb followed by the name of the file. The documentation says that, as with a script, the debugger pauses execution just before the first line of a module started this way (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript the program starts with a line def double(x): and the first thing the debugger prints is > main.py(1)<module>() followed by -> def double(x):. The first line names the file and the line number in parentheses, with <module> standing for the top level of the file, outside any function, and the second line shows the instruction that is about to run. The debugger then prints its prompt, (Pdb), and waits for a command. After the command n, which executes the current line and pauses at the next one in the same function, the next stop is on line 4, val = 3, because lines 2 and 3 belong to the function that line 1 only defines; after another n the stop is on line 5, result = double(val). Lines 2 and 3 run only when the function is called. This shows that the debugger moves through the lines in the order in which they execute, not the order in which they are written. Running under the debugger changes nothing about what the program does, only when it does it, so effects such as printing, asking for input, or writing a file all still happen. If the program ends, pdb reports that the program finished and will be restarted and stops again before the first line, as the executed run of the coin program shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And ending the session with the quit command aborts the program being executed, so lines after the stopping point never run.

slides.title: Program state
slides.say: A bug is a state that is not the one the programmer expected, and a wrong state always comes from some line. The chapter contrasts seeing the actual values in a program while it runs with having to deduce what the values might be from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Deduction can be wrong in exactly the places where the bug hides, whereas the state seen in the debugger is the real one. The skill of debugging is largely the skill of comparing the state that is shown with the state that was expected. The chapter's coin program is a good example of state. After 500 of the 1,000 flips, the variable i holds 500 and the variable heads holds the number of heads so far, which the programmer wanted to read at the halfway point (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript, a breakpoint on the line print('Halfway done!') followed by the command c stops there, and p i prints 500. The state also includes which line comes next, which pdb shows with an arrow after each stop. The state changes with every step. In the executed transcript of a two-line program that assigns x = 1 and then prints x, the command p x on line 1 prints *** NameError: name 'x' is not defined, because the line that creates x has not run yet; after the command n, p x prints 1. In a loop the state changes on every pass: with a breakpoint on the if line of the coin program, the first c stops with i equal to 1 and the second with i equal to 2. The state is only what is true now. A pause shows the value that a variable has at that moment and not the values it had before, so a wrong value found at a pause may have been created many steps earlier. The programmer then has to run again with an earlier breakpoint, or step through the earlier lines while watching the value. A state that looks right also proves little, since the bug may show itself only with other values.

slides.title: Debug Inspector pane
slides.say: The pane is where the debugger answers the question that logging and assertions can only answer in advance: what is in the variables now. In the chapter's adding program, the pane shows that the variables first, second and third hold the string values '5', '3' and '42' instead of the integer values 5, 3 and 42, and that is the whole bug (Sweigart, 2025). The quote marks around the values are the evidence. Without them the pane would show 5, 3 and 42 and the problem would stay hidden. In Mu the pane is shown beside the file editor throughout a debugging session, as in Figure 5-3 of the chapter. In pdb the same information is requested on demand with the command p followed by an expression, which prints the value of the expression in the current context (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript of a program that assigns first = '5', second = '3' and third = '42', the command p first prints '5' with its quote marks, and p first + second + third prints '5342'. The pane lets the programmer test a theory before changing anything. In the adding program the theory is that adding the three variables joins their text, and the evidence is the quote marks. The cure follows from it: int() turns each string into a number, and in the executed transcript p int(first) + int(second) + int(third) prints 50. In pdb the command p can take any expression, so the same session can answer many questions about the state of the program without editing the file. The pane shows values, but a value alone can mislead. The text '5' and the number 5 look alike unless the display shows the quote marks,. Also, the pane shows the program as it is when paused and says nothing about how it got there, so the programmer should step through the preceding lines while watching the value change. In pdb, asking for a variable that has not been assigned yet prints an error line that says the name is not defined.

slides.title: Stop button
slides.say: A debugging session can end before the program does, at the moment the answer is found. A student who has seen in the pane that a variable holds a string has no need to run the remaining lines, and may not want them to run at all if they would write a file or wait for further input. Stop is the control that says the session is over and the program should not go on, whereas Continue says the program should go on without the debugger's pauses. In Mu the button is on the top row of the editor. In pdb the command is q or quit, and an end-of-file on the input has the same effect (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript of a program that prints a line called end after its last statement, giving the command q at the first stop prints nothing of the program at all, because it never reached the print, and the output ends with the (Pdb) prompt. In 3.14 the documentation adds that a confirmation prompt is shown if the debugger was invoked in inline mode, which is the mode that breakpoint() uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The two ways of leaving a session differ in what happens to the rest of the program. Continue runs the rest of the program at full speed, stopping only at breakpoints (Sweigart, 2025). Stop terminates it. With pdb there is a third case, in which the program reaches its end by itself: pdb then reports that the program finished and will be restarted and returns to the first line, ready for another run (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Stopping is not the same as finishing. A program stopped in the middle may have printed only part of its output, written only part of a file, or changed things that the rest of the program would have changed back. And stopping the debugger does not remove the bug: the programmer still has to edit the program and run it again.

slides.title: Controls
slides.say: The controls are the means by which the programmer moves a paused program forward, or tells it where to pause. The chapter lists the buttons that Debugging mode adds to the editor: Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out (Sweigart, 2025). The fifth control is the breakpoint, a mark on a line that makes the program pause whenever it gets there. Every control answers the question of how far the program should run before it stops again. A debugger is only as useful as the control the programmer has over it. Stepping through a long program one line at a time takes too long, and running it at full speed lets the interesting moment go by. The chapter shows how the controls divide the work: breakpoints and Continue skip the part of the program that is not of interest, and the steps examine the part that is. The chapter notes, for instance, that stepping through the 1,000 flips of its coin program would take thousands of clicks (Sweigart, 2025). The controls are the buttons at the top of the Mu window, the entries of IDLE's debugger window, and the commands of pdb. The documentation of pdb names them step, next, return, continue and break, each also available in the short form s, n, r, c and b (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's questions at the end ask for exactly these differences between the three step buttons and for the moment at which Continue stops. The concepts come in this order: the breakpoint, which places a pause in the program, Continue, which runs to the next pause, and the three steps, which move by a line, over a call, or out of a function. For each control the text gives the button of Mu, the command of pdb, and an executed transcript on a small program in which a function named double is defined on line 1 and called on line 5. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Breakpoint
slides.say: Breakpoints solve the problem of speed. Stepping through the program with the debugger is helpful but can also be slow (Sweigart, 2025), and often the interesting moment is far from the start. The chapter's coin program flips a coin 1,000 times, and the question of interest is the value of heads at the halfway point, when 500 flips are done. With a breakpoint the program runs at full speed to that moment and stops there, where the clicking of Step Over thousands of times would otherwise be needed. In the chapter the breakpoint is placed on the line print('Halfway done!'), inside the if statement that checks whether i is 500. In the executed transcript of that program, the pdb command b 7 sets a breakpoint on line 7 and prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:7; the command c then runs the loop and stops at line 7, and the command p i prints 500 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation describes break as setting a break at a given line number in the current file. IDLE has the same facility through a context menu and, as its documentation says, saves the breakpoints of a file in the user's .idlerc directory (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The line matters. The chapter points out that a breakpoint on the if statement itself would stop at every pass through the loop, because that line runs on every iteration, whereas a breakpoint on the line inside the if stops only when the execution enters the if clause (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript a breakpoint on line 4, the if line, followed by two c commands, stops with i equal to 2, so each pass stopped once. After a stop the programmer can use Continue, Step Over, Step In or Step Out as normal (Sweigart, 2025). A breakpoint on a line that never runs never stops the program, and a breakpoint on a line that runs very often stops very often. In IDLE, the documentation says that breakpoints only have an effect when running under the debugger (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so a program started with the plain Run command ignores them. In IDLE the breakpoints of a file are kept in the .idlerc directory and not in the program file, so the saved program is unchanged. A line that holds no instruction cannot carry a breakpoint: in the executed transcript, b 5 on a blank line prints *** Blank or comment and sets nothing, while b 4 on the line before it prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:4. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Continue control
slides.say: Continue is the control that joins the two modes of work. Between breakpoints the programmer wants the program at full speed, and at a breakpoint the programmer wants it slowly. Without Continue, a debugging session would have to choose one or the other. With it, a session reads like a story: the program starts paused, Continue runs it up to the breakpoint, the programmer looks and steps, and Continue runs it up to the next one. In the chapter's coin program the program starts in a paused state at the first line, as usual, and clicking Continue makes it run at full speed until it reaches the line with the breakpoint (Sweigart, 2025). The executed transcript shows the same: after b 7 the command c ends with the stop at line 7, with the 500 flips behind it. If a second c is given, there is no further breakpoint, so the program runs on, prints its last lines, and pdb reports that the program finished and will be restarted. Continue stops for one of two reasons only: a breakpoint or the end of the program. If the same breakpoint is inside a loop, Continue stops again on every pass, and in the executed transcript of the breakpoint on the if line, the first c stopped at the first pass and the second c at the second. The chapter's last review question asks when the debugger stops after Continue, and the answer is just these two cases (Sweigart, 2025). Continue is not Stop. It leaves the debugger attached, and a breakpoint that is later reached pauses the program again, while Stop ends the session. And Continue offers no protection against a program that never ends: a loop that never finishes runs forever under Continue if no breakpoint is hit. In that case the programmer must interrupt the program or use the Stop button.

slides.title: Step in
slides.say: The control is for looking inside. When the value that arrives from a function call is wrong, the cause is either the arguments or the function, and Step In is how the programmer enters the function to find out which. It gives the finest view of a program, one line at a time through every call. The finest view is also the slowest, and the chapter therefore says that Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of the program that defines double on line 1 and calls it on line 5, the stops are line 1, line 4 and line 5. At line 5 the command s prints --Call-- and then > main.py(1)double() with -> def double(x):, so the debugger has entered the function and shows the name of the function in the place where <module> stood before. The word Call is how pdb marks a stop caused by entering a function. Step In behaves differently depending on the line. On a line that is not a call, it does the same as Step Over: it executes the line and pauses at the next. On a line that calls a function written in the program, it enters. The chapter notes that Mu should prevent the debugger from entering Python's built-in functions (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of pdb on a program whose lines 1 and 2 call print(), the command s on line 1 prints a and stops on line 2, so it did not enter print(). Step In on the wrong line leads into code that does not matter. The chapter warns about this with its adding program: the reader should use Step Over instead of Step In on the line that calls print(), because there is no interest in the code of print() (Sweigart, 2025). And once inside a function, the programmer must remember to get out again, with Step Out, or continue stepping through the lines of the function until it returns.

slides.title: Step over
slides.say: Most of the time the programmer knows which functions work and wants to follow the main line of the program. The chapter's example is a call of a function named spam() whose inside does not matter: Step Over runs it and pauses when it returns, and the chapter concludes that for this reason Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025). The control keeps the session short and the attention on the code under suspicion. In the adding program, the chapter uses Step Over for each of the print() and input() calls, from line 1 to the final print() on line 7, since stepping into the built-in functions would be pointless (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of the program with the function double, three n commands go from line 1 to line 4, to line 5 and to line 6, and after that the command p result prints 6. The call on line 5 ran completely in the third step, and the debugger never showed a stop inside the function. The control is a decision about detail. By choosing Step Over on a line, the programmer says that the result of the line matters but how it was computed does not. If the result later turns out to be wrong, the programmer can start again, or use the breakpoint, and choose Step In on that line. The stops of the debugger stay in the same function, the one that is being examined, and each stop is the next line of that function. Step Over hides what happens inside the call, including a bug. A function that has a mistake can return a wrong value, and Step Over will report only that the line finished. slides.title: Step over
slides.say: Most of the time the programmer knows which functions work and wants to follow the main line of the program. The chapter's example is a call of a function named spam() whose inside does not matter: Step Over runs it and pauses when it returns, and the chapter concludes that for this reason Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025). The control keeps the session short and the attention on the code under suspicion. In the adding program, the chapter uses Step Over for each of the print() and input() calls, from line 1 to the final print() on line 7, since stepping into the built-in functions would be pointless (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of the program with the function double, three n commands go from line 1 to line 4, to line 5 and to line 6, and after that the command p result prints 6. The call on line 5 ran completely in the third step, and the debugger never showed a stop inside the function. The control is a decision about detail. By choosing Step Over on a line, the programmer says that the result of the line matters but how it was computed does not. If the result later turns out to be wrong, the programmer can start again, or use the breakpoint, and choose Step In on that line. slides.title: Step out
slides.say: The control repairs a step that went too deep. After Step In the programmer is on the first line of a function. If it turns out that the function is not under suspicion, walking through every one of its lines is a waste, and Step Out spends them at full speed. It is the counterpart of Step In in the way that going back is the counterpart of going forward, and it is used less than Step Over because a careful programmer steps in only where it is wanted. In the executed transcript, the command s at line 5 enters the function double and stops on its first line, and the command r then prints --Return-- followed by > main.py(3)double()->6 and -> return y. The arrow and the number after it show that the function is about to return the value 6. The debugger has stopped on the return line, one step before control passes back to the caller, and one more step with n would continue in the calling code. Step Out is therefore a way of saying finish this function. It does not skip the lines that follow in the caller. A breakpoint on a line of the function that has not yet run still stops the program first: in the executed transcript a breakpoint is set on line 2 of double after stepping into it, and the command r then stops on line 2 and not at the return. After the stop at the return, pdb shows the value that the function returns after the arrow, so the programmer can see the result before it is used. Step Out from the top level, outside any function, has no function to leave. In the executed transcript the command r on line 1 of the program runs everything, so 6 and end are printed, and the stop is on the last line, where pdb prints --Return-- with ->None. The tools also differ in where they pause: the chapter speaks of executing at full speed until the function is left, and pdb pauses on the return line itself. The reader who needs the stop to be in the caller should take one more step.

slides.title: Python debugger
slides.say: The Python debugger is the debugger that comes with Python itself, the module pdb. The documentation says that pdb defines an interactive source code debugger for Python programs, with breakpoints, single stepping at the level of source lines, source code listing, and evaluation of Python code in the context of the paused program; it also supports post-mortem debugging, which means examining a program after it has crashed, and can be called under program control (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's controls all exist in it as commands. Unlike the buttons of an editor, pdb belongs to the standard library, so it comes with Python. It needs no window: the executed transcripts of this chapter were produced by starting it as a separate program and typing its commands as lines of input. It can be started in three ways: from the command line with python -m pdb followed by the file name, from inside the program by the function breakpoint(), and, since Python 3.14, by attaching to a process that is already running. The concepts below take the ways in turn. The module is met whenever a Python program is run with python -m pdb, and whenever breakpoint() is reached. Its prompt is (Pdb). The documentation also shows the case of a program that has crashed: pdb.pm() can be called afterwards to enter the debugger at the place where the exception occurred and to print the value of a variable there (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Started as a module, pdb enters this post-mortem mode automatically if the program exits abnormally; in the executed transcript of a program that divides by zero on its second line, pdb prints Uncaught exception. Entering post mortem debugging and stops on that line. The concepts of this group begin with the two ideas that the later ones depend on: the process, which is a running program, and the environment variable, a named setting handed to a program when it starts. They continue with the function breakpoint() and the hook that it calls, with the commands of pdb that correspond to the buttons of the chapter, and with attaching to a running process, which is new in Python 3.14. Use this slide to say what the next few slides are for before any of them appears: the table on the right is exactly the concepts that follow, each with the example the chapter uses for it. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Process
slides.say: The idea matters for debugging because running programs can be pointed at by number. A debugger that is started together with a program controls that one program. A debugger that attaches to a program that is already running needs to know which one, and the process identifier is the answer. The process identifier is met in the command python -m pdb -p 1234 and in the call sys.remote_exec(1234, script) of Python 3.14 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed expression isinstance(os.getpid(), int) evaluates to True, and os.getpid() > 0 does too. Two runs of Python are two processes even if they run the same file. The documentation of the subprocess module says that it allows a program to spawn new processes (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and a process spawned in this way has an identifier of its own: in the executed check, the number printed by the child differs from the number of the parent. A process also has an environment, which is the subject of the next concept. The identifier belongs to one run only, since two runs are two processes. A tool that is pointed at a wrong number would examine another program, so the number should be read from the program itself, for example by printing os.getpid(), at the time it is needed. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Environment variable
slides.say: Environment variables let a user change how a program behaves without editing it. For debugging this is valuable: the same program file can be run with its breakpoints active on one day and switched off on the next, and the file does not change. Python's own settings use the same means. The variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT, which is the subject of the following concepts, decides what the function breakpoint() does. In os.environ, the executed expression type(os.environ).__name__ evaluates to '_Environ', the class that holds the environment. A program reads a variable with os.environ.get('NAME'), which gives None when the variable is not set; the executed check prints None for a name that is not set. The documentation also says that the mapping may be used to modify the environment, and the executed check shows that a variable assigned in os.environ is visible to a child process that is started afterwards (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation says that the mapping is captured the first time the os module is imported, typically during Python startup, and that changes made to the environment after this time are not reflected in os.environ, except for changes made by modifying os.environ directly (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that changes os.environ changes the environment that it passes on: in the executed check the parent sets GREETING to hi and the child that is started next prints hi, while 'GREETING' in os.environ is True in the parent. Values are text. The documentation says that keys and values are strings, so a setting such as 0 is the string '0', not the number zero (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It adds that on Windows the keys are converted to upper case, so a name written in lower case is stored in upper case there (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And a program that wants a value must handle its absence: os.environ.get('NAME') returns None when the variable is not set, but os.environ['NAME'] has no such default. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Breakpoint function
slides.say: PEP 553 lists the disadvantages of the older idiom: it is a lot to type (27 characters), it is easy to mistype, and it ties debugging directly to the choice of pdb (Warsaw, 2017). The new function is short, and because it does not name pdb, the debugger that it starts can be chosen without changing the program. The PEP adds that even where an editor has a user interface for setting breakpoints, it may still be more convenient to just edit the code (Warsaw, 2017). The function is used in scripts, and the pdb page of the documentation shows an example in which breakpoint() is the first line of a function double, followed by a session in which p x prints 3 and continue lets the program finish (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed run of a small program that prints before, calls breakpoint() and then prints after, the output contains before, then a (Pdb) prompt, and, after the command c, the word after. The function does little itself. It calls sys.breakpointhook(), passing on whatever arguments it received, and returns what the hook returns (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The default hook starts pdb at the line after the call. The function therefore behaves as the hook decides, which the next concept explains. The executed expression sys.breakpointhook.__name__ evaluates to 'breakpointhook', the default hook that breakpoint() calls. A breakpoint() that is left in the program will stop it for whoever runs it, including users who have no one to type commands. It should be removed before the program is shared, or switched off with the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, for which the executed run prints before and then the program went on without any pause. The documentation also says that if sys.breakpointhook cannot be reached, breakpoint() raises RuntimeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And since the default hook starts pdb.set_trace(), which expects no arguments, calling breakpoint(1) raises a TypeError, as the executed check shows. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Breakpoint hook
slides.say: A hook lets one line of code, breakpoint(), serve many debuggers. A programmer who prefers another debugger can set the hook once, and the programs need not change. The environment variable also lets the person who runs the program turn the call off. The default hook consults PYTHONBREAKPOINT: if it is set to 0, the hook returns at once and does nothing; if it is not set or is empty, pdb.set_trace() is called; otherwise the variable names a function to call, in the dotted form package.module.function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed runs show each case. With PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, a program that prints before, calls breakpoint() and prints the program went on shows no pause. With PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to builtins.print, breakpoint('hello', 'hook') prints hello hook, because the named function receives the arguments that were passed. And a program that assigns its own function to sys.breakpointhook has that function called, with its arguments, and breakpoint() returns what the function returns. The environment variable is read each time the default hook is called. If it names something that cannot be imported, the documentation says a RuntimeWarning is reported and the breakpoint is ignored (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed run, with PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to no.such.module.func, the error output ends with RuntimeWarning: Ignoring unimportable $PYTHONBREAKPOINT: "no.such.module.func", and the program carries on, printing went on. A program that replaces sys.breakpointhook by its own function no longer consults PYTHONBREAKPOINT, as the documentation says; in the executed run the replaced hook still ran with the variable set to 0 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And the setting 0 silences only breakpoint(): in the executed transcript, with PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, the command b 2 inside pdb still stops the program on line 2.

slides.title: Pdb commands
slides.say: The commands make the controls of the chapter available in a terminal and in scripts, and they add to them. The command p expression evaluates an expression in the current context and prints its value, so it does the work of the Debug Inspector pane. The command where prints a stack trace with the most recent frame at the bottom and an arrow marking the current frame, which is the call stack of Chapter 4 viewed from the debugger (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The command list shows 11 lines of source code around the current line, with -> marking the current line (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcripts every control of the chapter appears as a command: n and s give the stops on lines 4 and 5 and then --Call-- at the start of double; r gives --Return-- and the value 6; b 6 prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:6, and c stops there, where p result prints 6. The check on the class Pdb confirms that the six methods do_step, do_next, do_return, do_continue, do_break and do_where exist, which is the evaluated io example of this concept. The commands steer the paused program, and a statement written after an exclamation point is executed in its context; the point can be omitted unless the first word of the statement resembles a debugger command (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation says that print() can also be used, but it is not a debugger command and executes the Python print() function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The command-line form python -m pdb [-c command] file starts the program paused at the first line, and -c runs commands as if they were in a .pdbrc file (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A name that matches a command is read as the command: the documentation says the exclamation point can be omitted only unless the first word resembles a debugger command (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript a variable called c holds 5, and p c prints 5, whereas typing c alone is the command continue and the program ran on to its end. Before a variable has been assigned, p prints an error line: p x on line 1 of a program that assigns x on that line prints *** NameError: name 'x' is not defined. slides.title: Remote attach
slides.say: PEP 768 states the need: developers often need to analyze application behavior without stopping or restarting services, which is especially crucial for high-availability systems, and very few Python tools could attach to running processes (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024). The What's New page for 3.14 calls the new interface a crucial capability for high-availability systems and production environments, since tools can inspect and interact with Python applications in real time (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The interface is used by debuggers and other tools, and the documented command is python -m pdb -p followed by the number of the process. The function sys.remote_exec is available on Unix and Windows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed demonstration starts a child program that prints ready and then sleeps; the parent calls sys.remote_exec on its identifier with a script that prints injected, and the child's output then contains injected. On a Python older than 3.14 the function does not exist, so there is nothing to call. The function returns at once, and the code is run by the main thread of the target process at the next available opportunity; there is no interface to learn when it ran, and the caller must keep the file in place until it has (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The target must run the same major and minor version of CPython as the caller (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation of pdb adds that a process blocked in a system call or waiting for I/O attaches only once the next bytecode instruction is executed, and the glossary defines bytecode as the internal representation of a Python program in the CPython interpreter (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The same power is a risk, since a tool that can run code in another process could be misused, so the feature can be disabled: with the environment variable PYTHON_DISABLE_REMOTE_DEBUG, with the option -X disable-remote-debug, or at build time with --without-remote-debug (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It also needs the same version on both sides. The runnable example of this concept is deliberately small: it checks only that sys.breakpointhook is callable, because attaching needs a second running process of the same version and cannot be shown in one expression. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Modern practice
slides.say: Modern practice is the part of the chapter in which the four instruments, exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger, are used together on programs that contain real mistakes. The chapter does this three times. It repairs a factorial function with the help of log messages, it finds why an adding program prints a wrong sum with the help of the debugger, and it ends with a practice program, a coin toss guessing game that the author says has multiple bugs in it, to be found by running the program a few times (Sweigart, 2025). The word modern points to the tools of current Python, which the other branches describe one by one. Knowing what an instrument does is not yet knowing when to use it. A learner who has read about the debugger still has to decide, faced with a program that prints the wrong number, whether to print values, to add a check or to step through the lines. The practice cases give that decision a concrete setting. The chapter's own advice is that, in general, the earlier you catch bugs, the easier they will be to fix (Sweigart, 2025), and a worked case shows what catching a bug early looks like in a real program. The cases are met in the chapter's three programs and in the programs a learner writes afterwards. A loop that starts at the wrong number, a running total that begins with the wrong value, input that arrives as text instead of numbers, a random number that is compared with a word, and a test of membership applied to the wrong kind of value all appear in programs of a few lines. Each of these has a name in this branch and a short executed example. The branch has one group, the worked cases. Each case names a kind of mistake, shows the symptom that it produces, shows the evidence that exposes it and states the repair. The first two cases, the off-by-one range and the starting value of an accumulator, belong to the factorial. The third, string concatenation, belongs to the adding program. The last three, the random integer, the membership test and the type mismatch comparison, belong to the coin toss game. The cases are exercises in reading evidence, and the evidence is always a value that is not the one expected. A case is a pattern and not a recipe. The same symptom can have several causes: a total of zero can come from a loop that starts at zero, but also from a running total that was started at zero when a product was meant. The repair that fits one program may be wrong for the next one. The cases also do not replace testing; they train the eye for the evidence, and the evidence has to be produced by running the program. This divider is the branch's own description from the chapter corpus; the boxes under it name every concept in the branch, so the room can see how far there is to go.

slides.title: Worked cases
slides.say: The worked cases are six small mistakes, each taken from one of the programs of the chapter. A case consists of the faulty line, the symptom that the program shows, the instrument that exposes the cause, and the repair. Most of the cases produce no error message at all, which makes them logic errors; two of them, the ordering comparison and the membership test on a string, show an error message when the same mistake is pushed a little further. The cases are useful in three ways. They show how each instrument is used on a real program and not on an artificial one. They give the learner a stock of patterns to recognise, which shortens the search the next time. And they fix the vocabulary: to say that a bug is an off-by-one in a range, or a type mismatch in a comparison, is to say where to look. In the chapter the logging output pointed at the range, and the debugger pane at the strings. The cases follow the order of the chapter's programs. The off-by-one range and the accumulator starting value explain the factorial that returns 0. String concatenation explains the adding program, whose pane shows '5', '3' and '42' as strings. The random integer, the membership test and the type mismatch comparison explain the lines of the coin toss game that decide whether the player's guess is accepted and whether it matches. For each case the executed examples show the value that exposes the mistake. Click the rows in one at a time if the room is new to the material.

slides.title: Off-by-one range
slides.say: The error is easy to make because the counting rules of ranges are not the counting rules of everyday speech. People count from 1 and include the last number, and range counts from 0 by default and leaves the last number out. A programmer who writes range(n + 1) has remembered that the last number is left out and added 1 to make up for it, but forgot that the first number is 0. The mistake produces no error message: the program runs and prints 0, which the chapter calls a result that isn't right (Sweigart, 2025). The log in the chapter shows the evidence. The debug messages say i is 0, total is 0 on the first pass, and then total stays 0 on every pass because zero times anything is zero (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed program, factorial(5) with range(n + 1) prints 0, and with range(1, n + 1) it prints 120. The two ranges are visible directly: list(range(5 + 1)) is [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], list(range(1, 5 + 1)) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], and range(0) is empty. The repair changes the first number of the range. With range(1, n + 1) the loop variable i takes the values 1 to n, and the log of the chapter then shows i and total as 1 and 1, 2 and 2, 3 and 6, 4 and 24, and 5 and 120 (Sweigart, 2025). The number of passes matters as much as their values: len(range(5 + 1)) is 6, one more than the 5 that len(range(1, 5 + 1)) gives, and the first pass was the harmful one. In the executed check factorial(0) and factorial(1) both give 1 after the repair, as the mathematical definition requires. Counting errors hide in the edges. An off-by-one error can show itself only for the first or the last item, so tests should use the smallest case, the case with one item, and the case with none. A repair that adds or subtracts 1 until the output looks right is dangerous; the right question is which numbers the loop should visit, and the answer should be written down before the range. Watching the first and last pass in a log or in the debugger is the quickest check. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Accumulator starting value
slides.say: The starting value is part of the logic of the program, and a wrong one gives a wrong answer without any error. A product must start with 1, because multiplying by 1 changes nothing, and a sum must start with 0, because adding 0 changes nothing. A product that starts with 0 stays 0, and a sum that starts with 1 comes out one too large. The starting value is a place where a logic error can live, since the loop looks right and only the line before it is wrong. Accumulators appear in nearly every program that totals, counts or builds a result. In the executed examples, a loop that adds the numbers 1 to 5 to a total that starts at 0 gives 15; the same loop with the total starting at 1 gives 16; and a loop that multiplies the numbers 1 to 5 into a total that starts at 0 gives 0, the same wrong answer as the chapter's factorial, though here the cause is the starting value and not the range. The built-in sum(range(1, 5 + 1)) evaluates to 15 and checks the first result. The update line works in the same way on every pass: it takes the current value, combines it with the item, and stores the result back. The statement x += 1 can be rewritten as x = x + 1 to achieve a similar, but not exactly equal, effect, because the augmented form evaluates x only once (Python Software Foundation, 2026). After the loop the accumulator holds the result. To check one, the programmer can print it inside the loop, as the chapter does with its log messages, or can set a breakpoint on the update line and read the value on each pass. When a total comes out wrong, there are two suspects, the loop and the starting value, and both must be checked before anything is changed. Another trap is to initialise the accumulator inside the loop, which resets it on every pass and leaves only the last item. And the type of the accumulator matters: the same update written with + on strings joins text, as in the next case, instead of adding numbers. After the loop the accumulator holds the result. To check one, the programmer can print it inside the loop, as the chapter does with its log messages, or can set a breakpoint on the update line and read the value on each pass. When a total comes out wrong, there are two suspects, the loop and the starting value, and both must be checked before anything is changed. Another trap is to initialise the accumulator inside the loop, which resets it on every pass and leaves only the last item. And the type of the accumulator matters: the same update written with + on strings joins text, as in the next case, instead of adding numbers. slides.title: String concatenation
slides.say: The case matters because the data that input() returns is always text. The documentation of input() says that the function reads a line from input, converts it to a string, and returns that (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that asks a person for numbers therefore holds strings, and the programmer sees the digits and takes them for numbers. The chapter's Debug Inspector pane makes the difference visible: the variables first, second and third are set to '5', '3' and '42' instead of 5, 3 and 42, and when the last line is executed Python concatenates the strings instead of adding the numbers (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed program the three answers are read with input(), and print('The sum is ' + first + second + third) prints The sum is 5342, while converting each answer with int() gives 50. The types can be read directly: type(input()).__name__ is 'str' even when the line typed was 7. The multiplication sign shows the same difference, since '5' * 3 is '555' and 5 * 3 is 15. And mixing the two kinds fails: adding a string and a number raises a TypeError, whose message for 'The sum is ' + 5 is can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. The cure is to convert before computing. The function int() turns a string of digits into an integer, so int(first) + int(second) + int(third) is the sum that was meant. The debugger shows the cure at work: in the pdb transcript of the adding program, p first + second + third prints '5342' and p int(first) + int(second) + int(third) prints 50. A conversion done right after the input call keeps the rest of the program working with numbers. Conversion has its own failure: int() applied to a string that is not made of digits raises a ValueError, so a check on the input belongs near the input call. The quote marks in the display of a value are the most reliable sign that it is a string, and the debugger shows them where print() does not: print(first) shows 5, and the pane shows '5'. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Random integer
slides.say: Chance is useful in programs that simulate, shuffle or play games, and it makes debugging harder, because a bug may show itself on one run and not on the next. The chapter's coin program therefore prints a different count each time: the book shows 490 heads in one run (Sweigart, 2025). A programmer who wants a repeatable run can call random.seed, which the documentation describes as initialising the random number generator (Python Software Foundation, 2026); in the executed check, two runs seeded with 1 give the same five numbers. The coin flip in the chapter calls random.randint(0, 1) a thousand times and counts the ones as heads. The practice program calls it once, in toss = random.randint(0, 1), with the comment that 0 is tails and 1 is heads (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed checks, randint(5, 5) always returns 5, because the two ends are the same; randint(1, 3) over 500 calls produced exactly the numbers 1, 2 and 3; and the values are integers, so isinstance(random.randint(1, 6), int) is True and the type is int, not str. The function needs the first number not to be larger than the second. In the executed check, random.randint(2, 1) raises a ValueError whose message begins empty range in. Under Python 3.14 the message ends with randint(2, 1), and under Python 3.12 it ends with randrange(2, 2), which shows the documented alias at work: randint(a, b) is randrange(a, b + 1) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A coin flip is a choice between two numbers, and the program must decide what each number means: here 0 stands for tails and 1 for heads, and nothing in the number itself says so. The result is a number and not a word. A program that compares it with a string, as the practice program does, will never find them equal, which is the last of the worked cases. The random values are also not guaranteed to balance: the book's own run printed 490 heads in 1,000 flips, not 500 (Sweigart, 2025). And a breakpoint at the halfway point of such a program shows a different value of the counter on every run. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Membership test
slides.say: The test replaces a chain of comparisons with one readable condition. Without it the loop would have to say guess != 'heads' and guess != 'tails', and a third answer would lengthen the line. For strings the operator means something else: the language reference says that for the string types x in y is True if and only if x is a substring of y (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Both meanings are useful, and mixing them up is the source of a typical mistake. In the practice program the test works as intended. In the executed run with the inputs maybe, tails and tails, the question Guess the coin toss! Enter heads or tails: is printed twice, once for maybe, which is not a member of the tuple, and once for tails, which is. The difference between the two meanings is visible in the checks: 'ab' in 'abc' is True because it is a substring, 'head' in 'heads' is True, but 'head' in ('heads', 'tails') is False because 'head' is not a member of the tuple. The two sides of the operator must fit. A string on the right accepts only strings on the left, and the check 1 in 'abc' raises a TypeError with the message 'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not int. A tuple on the right accepts any value, and the test uses equality, so 0 in (0, 1) is True and '0' in (0, 1) is False. A single value in parentheses is not a tuple: the check type(('heads')).__name__ gives 'str', and type(('heads',)).__name__ gives 'tuple', because the comma makes the tuple (Python Software Foundation, 2026). One error to watch for is forgetting the comma. With guess in ('heads') the test asks whether guess is a substring of the word heads, so the answer 'he' is accepted. A second trap is to write the test as guess == 'heads' or 'tails', which is true for every guess, because a string that is not empty counts as true when it is used as a condition (Python Software Foundation, 2026); in the executed check the expression 'x' == 'heads' or 'tails' evaluates to 'tails', which is true. The membership operator avoids both. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Type mismatch comparison
slides.say: The mistake is silent and total. The program runs, asks its questions, and answers Nope! to every guess, the correct one too. Nothing is raised and nothing is logged. The only evidence is the behaviour: the executed run with the inputs heads and heads prints Nope! Guess again! and then Nope. You are really bad at this game., and a player who guesses for ever is never right. The case shows why the chapter calls the program one with multiple bugs in it, to be found by running it a few times (Sweigart, 2025). The comparison appears wherever data arrives in one form and is tested in another, as the number from randint and the word typed by the player do. The ordering operators are stricter than equality: the language reference says a default order comparison is not provided and an attempt raises TypeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and in the executed check 0 < 'heads' raises a TypeError with the message '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'. Equality asks only whether the values are the same and answers no, while ordering asks which is larger and cannot answer. The repair is to compare like with like. Either the number is turned into the word, as in ['tails', 'heads'][toss], which gives 'heads' for 1 and 'tails' for 0, or the word is turned into the number. The program's own comment says that 0 is tails and 1 is heads, and the comment states exactly the mapping that the code has to carry out. The check can be made with p toss == guess in the debugger or with a temporary print of both values and their types. A correct-looking condition is not evidence. A program that prints Nope for every input should lead the programmer to print the two operands and their types, not to read the condition again. The mismatch can also stand in a place where the comparison is spread over lines or functions, so that the two values never appear together. Also remember that numbers of different types do compare, since a comparison between numbers of different types behaves as though the exact values were compared (Python Software Foundation, 2026): 1 == 1.0 is True, so the rule concerns kinds that are unrelated, such as number and string. Every printed result on this slide was produced by running the code under Python 3.14.4.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 1. What question do raising exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger all answer in different ways? The answer is: How can the programmer find out what the program is really doing? The branch presents the four instruments as four answers to one question: what the program is really doing, as opposed to what its source appears to say. 2. A program runs to its end, prints a plausible result, and the result is wrong. What kind of bug is it? The answer is: A logic error, which Python does not report A logic error lets the program run without any exception, so only a person who knows the right answer notices it. 3. What is a bug, in the sense of the chapter? The answer is: A place where the program does something other than its author intended A bug is the gap between the intention of the programmer and the behaviour of the running program; the computer carries out the instructions exactly as written. 4. What does the traceback of an unhandled exception tell the person who runs the program? The answer is: That something went wrong, and the calls the exception passed through Raising an exception and the traceback it prints are how a program says that something went wrong, and the traceback records where the exception passed. 5. A function cannot serve a call it was given. What does raising an exception let the function do? The answer is: Refuse the call and let the caller decide how to recover Raising shows how a function refuses a call it cannot serve and how the caller then recovers. Let the room answer before each click. The full bank of 128 questions for this chapter, with a reason for every wrong option, is on the chapter page.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.say: 6. What does a raise statement do to the running code? The answer is: It stops the code and passes an exception to the nearest matching except clause A raise statement stops the running code and hands the exception to the nearest matching except clause, which is how a function tells its caller that a call was invalid. 7. Whose errors are assertions meant to catch? The answer is: The programmer's errors, meaning bugs in the code Assertions are sanity checks meant for errors of the programmer and not of the user. 8. What does an assertion state? The answer is: What must be true at that point if the program is correct An assertion states what must be true at a point in a program. 9. What does a sanity check test? The answer is: A property that must hold if the code before it is correct A sanity check is a cheap test of a result that must hold if the preceding code did its job, written to catch an obvious mistake early. 10. What is logging for? The answer is: Leaving a record of what a program did without stopping it Logging leaves a record of what a program did, without stopping it. Let the room answer before each click. The full bank of 128 questions for this chapter, with a reason for every wrong option, is on the chapter page.

slides.title: Check yourself

For which kind of question is the debugger the right instrument? The answer is: What the variables hold at one particular line The debugger is the instrument for a question about the state at one line. 14. Which part of the Mu window lists the current values of the program's variables? The answer is: The Debug Inspector pane The Debug Inspector pane opens at the right side of the window and lists the current value of the variables of the program. 15. Which button of the Mu editor starts a program under the debugger? The answer is: Debug The Debug button in the top row, next to the Run button, starts the program under the debugger.
